text: A find's story needs more than a photo
Today we will learn why a find needs a record of where it was found.
Your goal is to explain why place and layer records matter.
Explain why place and layer records matter, and choose a careful way to protect a find.
Context means a find?s recorded place, layer and relationships to other finds. These details help connect the object to its setting.

A photograph shows a stone tool. A field note records its cave and layer. The photo shows what the tool looks like; the note connects it to where it was found. Together they tell us more than the photo alone.
Read the three evidence notes
Open each note. Ask yourself: what does this information help us understand?
Open a note, then tap Listen to hear it.
Place
A place record tells us where a find was noticed. Tabon is in Quezon, Palawan. Callao Cave is in Peñablanca, Cagayan. They are different sites.
Why it matters.
Keep a find with its correct site label. A map locates a site; it does not, by itself, prove how ancient people travelled.
Layer and surroundings
A layer record describes the layer and relationships to other finds. These details are part of the find’s context.
A photograph can show the object’s appearance. It cannot replace a record of its layer and surroundings.
Care
At a managed heritage site, leave a possible old object in place and notify responsible site staff. Let staff decide how to record and handle it.
Moving or washing an object can disturb the information around it. Protecting the setting protects opportunities to learn.
Protect the evidence
You notice a possible old object at a managed heritage site. Move the steps into a careful order, then check your plan.
Recording a find helps most when its setting is still undisturbed. Leave it in place before telling staff. Moving the object first can separate it from useful information.
Notify responsible site staff.
Let responsible staff record its setting.
Leave the object where it is.
Explain why the notes matter
A museum has a photograph of a find, but no record of its place or layer. Which explanation uses what you learned?
A. A clear photograph can replace the missing place and layer records.
B. Without its place and layer notes, we know less about the find.
C. The missing notes do not matter if the object looks very old.
What will you remember?
A photograph shows appearance. Context connects the find to its recorded setting. Both can help us learn about the past.
Context includes recorded place, layer and relationships to other finds.
A photograph helps show appearance. It does not replace the setting records.
At a managed heritage site, leave a possible find in place and notify responsible staff.
You arrive in an early Filipino community, where Bayani, your time-travel learning guide, welcomes you.
“Explorer! I need your help,” Bayani says. “Let's discover how people in this community make important decisions.”
You follow Bayani to a gathering place. Two families are talking about a disagreement. They have different ideas about how to solve a problem.
The datu listens as each family explains its concerns.
“Why doesn't the datu decide right away?” you whisper.
“Understanding the problem is important,” Bayani replies. “In some early Filipino communities, leaders listened to others and considered local customs before making decisions.”
The datu asks questions, and the families explain their views.
Bayani turns to you.
“Your first discovery is about leadership. What can we learn from the way people handle this disagreement?”
You look closely. Your journey into early Filipino society has begun!

People could do similar work but have different rights and choices. Social position means a recognized place in society. It could affect what someone was expected to do and what they were free to choose.

One example comes from Juan de Plasencia, a Spanish missionary writing about Tagalog communities in 1589. His account was written after Spanish arrival. It does not describe every Philippine community.
